name: Misleading bar chart ad
description: An ad that makes a small difference look enormous by starting the axis high, backed by a tiny sample the advertiser paid for.
trap: Truncated axis and a biased sample
subject: Ads and media
generation_instructions:
Write a short advertisement for an invented product related to the topic.

The chart must contain the trap:
- Set y_min well above 0 (for example 80 when the values are 85 and 90) so a small real gap looks enormous.
- Give the advertised product a highlight bar and one rival a plain bar. Two or three bars only.
- Put the sample size and who paid for the study in the footnote, and make the sample small (under 30 people).
- Set the annotation to a short note pointing at the axis, e.g. "Axis starts at 80%, not 0%."

The body should read like confident ad copy that never mentions the axis or the sample size. Do not explain the trick anywhere a student can see it. Put the explanation only in thinking_trap.

The transcript should be four short lines from an interview where someone lets slip how few people were asked.

offline_draft.title: Students Are Choosing {brand}
offline_draft.subject: Ads and media
offline_draft.blurb: An ad about {topic} says {brand} beats the leading brand. The bar chart looks convincing.
offline_draft.intro: This ad for {topic} ran on a poster outside the school gym.
offline_draft.body: {brand} is what students pick when it comes to {topic}. We asked students at our sample tent which one worked better for them. {high}% said {brand} was the one that helped. Only {low}% said the same about the leading brand. Look at the chart and you can see the difference for yourself. The bar for {brand} towers over the competition. If you want the better option this semester, the choice is obvious. Ask for {brand} by name.
offline_draft.opening_prompt: Read the ad and look at the chart. What is one question you would ask before you believe it? You can highlight a sentence or click a part of the chart to show what you mean.
offline_draft.thinking_trap: Two tricks stack here. The y-axis starts at 80% instead of 0%, so a {gap}-point difference fills most of the chart and makes the bar look about twice as tall. And the sample is {n} students recruited at the company's own tent, paid for by the company, so it is both tiny and biased toward people who already liked {brand}.
offline_draft.chart_alt: A bar chart comparing two options. The {brand} bar looks about twice as tall as the leading brand, but the numbers up the side start at 80% instead of 0%.

chart.title: Students who say it worked better for them
chart.footnote: Based on {n} students at the {brand} tent. Funded by {brand}.

transcript.text: Interviewer: How did you pick the students for the survey?
Rep: We asked whoever stopped by our tent for a free sample.
Interviewer: And how many people was that?
Rep: {n}. But they were really enthusiastic.
